name: Gardner's Multiple Intelligences
statement: Gardner argued intelligence is not one thing but several, from linguistic to musical to interpersonal.
statementAccent: intelligence is not one thing but several
meaning: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences is a model of the mind proposed by the American developmental psychologist Howard Gardner in his 1983 book Frames of Mind, which argues that human intelligence is not a single general ability but a set of several relatively independent intelligences. Gardner challenged the traditional idea of intelligence as one thing, measured by a single IQ or captured by a general factor, and instead proposed that people possess distinct kinds of intelligence that can vary independently within a person. He originally described seven: linguistic, or verbal; logical-mathematical; musical; bodily-kinesthetic; spatial; interpersonal, the understanding of other people; and intrapersonal, the understanding of oneself. He later added an eighth, naturalistic intelligence, the ability to recognize and categorize the natural world, and has discussed a possible ninth, existential intelligence, without formally adopting it. The theory became enormously popular in education, where it encouraged teaching to students' diverse strengths and broadened the notion of what it means to be smart beyond narrow academic measures. It is influential and appealing, but it is also widely criticized by intelligence researchers for lacking strong empirical support.
mechanism: Gardner arrived at his intelligences not through factor analysis of test scores, the usual method of intelligence research, but by synthesizing evidence from many sources, including the study of prodigies and savants, brain damage that spares some abilities while impairing others, developmental trajectories, and the valued skills of different cultures. From criteria such as whether an ability can be selectively lost through brain injury or shown to unusual degree in special individuals, he argued that the mind comprises several semi-autonomous intelligences rather than one general capacity. Each intelligence is a distinct way of processing information and solving problems: linguistic intelligence handles language, logical-mathematical intelligence handles reasoning and number, musical intelligence handles rhythm and tone, bodily-kinesthetic intelligence handles movement and physical skill, spatial intelligence handles visual and spatial relationships, interpersonal intelligence handles understanding and interacting with others, and intrapersonal intelligence handles understanding oneself, with naturalistic intelligence added for recognizing patterns in nature. A person has a profile across all of them, strong in some and weaker in others, rather than a single overall level. In education, teachers use the framework to present material in multiple ways and to recognize and develop different strengths. The claim that the intelligences are genuinely independent, however, is where the theory meets its strongest scientific challenge.

whyItMatters: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences is one of the most popular and widely known ideas in modern education, because it challenged the narrow view of intelligence as a single ability measured by IQ tests and proposed instead that people are smart in many different ways. This broadened and humanized the notion of intelligence, encouraging educators to recognize and cultivate the diverse strengths of their students, whether linguistic, musical, spatial, physical, interpersonal, or other, and to teach material through multiple approaches rather than privileging only verbal and mathematical ability. The theory resonated strongly with teachers and shaped classroom practice, curriculum design, and educational philosophy around the world, offering a more inclusive picture of human potential. At the same time, the theory is scientifically important as a case study in the tension between an idea's popularity and its empirical support, since intelligence researchers have criticized it heavily for lacking validating evidence and for relabeling talents and abilities as intelligences. Whether one accepts or rejects it, Gardner's theory forced a valuable debate about what intelligence is and how schools should nurture it.

limits: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences is far more accepted in education than in scientific psychology, and this gap must be stated honestly. Intelligence researchers and psychometricians criticize it for lacking strong empirical support, noting that Gardner did not derive it from data in the usual way and that there is no validated test of the intelligences. Critics argue that what Gardner calls intelligences are better described as talents, abilities, or personality traits, and, crucially, that the intelligences are not truly independent, since scores on diverse cognitive tests consistently correlate, pointing to a general factor of intelligence that the theory downplays. The theory is also hard to test and has been called effectively unfalsifiable. It should not be confused with the related but distinct and largely discredited idea of learning styles, which Gardner himself has criticized.
misreadings: Gardner's multiple intelligences is not an empirically established scientific theory; it is popular in education but widely criticized by intelligence researchers for lacking validating evidence. The intelligences are not truly independent, since cognitive abilities consistently correlate, pointing to a general factor the theory downplays. And it is not the same as learning styles, a distinct and largely debunked idea that Gardner himself rejects, so treating multiple intelligences as settled science, as fully independent abilities, or as identical to learning styles, misreads an influential but contested theory of ability.
origin: A model of the mind proposed by the American developmental psychologist Howard Gardner in his 1983 book Frames of Mind, arguing that intelligence comprises several relatively independent intelligences rather than one general ability.
